title: Down the wall in a basket (Acts 9:20–31)
word: Down the wall in a basket
hookLine: a hunted man lowered over a wall at night, then one friend who says: he's with me
tomorrow: how do you show who someone was, without a speech?

lines: THE GATES WATCHED DAY AND NIGHT.
cards: First day somewhere new: a team, a lunch table, a job. Everyone already has a seat, and it helps more than anything when one person says, they're with me. Saul is about to need that.
Straight away he's in the synagogues of Damascus, saying Jesus is the Son of God, and everyone is amazed: isn't this the man who came to arrest the people who call on that name?

After many days, some in the city plot to kill him, and the gates are watched day and night. So how does a hunted man get out? "Then the disciples took him by night, and let him down by the wall in a basket."

teach.b: Here's the thing to tell a friend: Paul tells this story himself, in his second letter to the Corinthians, and he files it under his weaknesses, not his victories: "through a window in a basket was I let down by the wall, and escaped his hands."
A grown man folded into a basket in the dark. Then Jerusalem, and a harder wall.

teach.h: THEY WERE ALL AFRAID OF HIM.
teach.b: He tries to join the disciples, "but they were all afraid of him, and believed not that he was a disciple." It's hard to blame them; the last they knew, he was dragging believers off to prison. Then one man steps forward.
"But Barnabas took him, and brought him to the apostles, and declared unto them how he had seen the Lord in the way."
Barnabas, the son of consolation, who once laid the money from his land at the apostles' feet, now lays down something else: his own good name.
He tells Saul's story for him, when Saul's story is the very thing that scares them. Saul is welcomed, speaks boldly in Jerusalem, and when a new threat comes, the believers send him home to Tarsus.
Then Acts exhales: "Then had the churches rest."

teach.h: A BASKET AT NIGHT, A FRIEND BY DAY.
teach.b: A basket at night, a friend by day.
Both carried Saul where he couldn't go alone.

how: In some churches a newcomer to baptism or membership has a sponsor or godparent, someone who stands beside them and speaks for them.

games.q: what does “down the wall in a basket” mean?
o: how Joseph was pulled up from a dry pit
how baby Moses was hidden on the Nile
how Saul escaped Damascus, lowered by night

games.q: out of Damascus, into Jerusalem — tap the pairs.
p: let him down by the wall
where the believers sent Saul home

s: Paul told the basket story as a daring escape to be proud of
in 2 Corinthians he lists it among his weaknesses.
the disciples in Jerusalem welcomed Saul right away
they were all afraid of him, until Barnabas spoke for him.
Barnabas told the apostles how Saul had seen the Lord
he declared it for him, putting his own good name behind Saul's story.

games.q: a quiet new kid has started coming to your youth group, and some families are wary of him. you know him a little. what's the Barnabas move?
o: walk him in, introduce him by name, and say what you know of him.
wait until he proves himself, then say something kind about him.
tell him people are wary, so he knows to try harder.
games.why: Barnabas didn't wait for Saul to earn trust. he took him, brought him to the apostles, and told his story for him.

practice: Bring to mind one person new in your world who doesn't yet have anyone speaking for them. Name what you'd want for them: a seat, a friend, a fair hearing. Name what's in the way, maybe just your own nerves.
Then choose the first plain step, like walking them over and saying their name, and hold it in mind as you breathe.

wordCard.voice: Down the wall in a basket. How Saul left Damascus by night, lowered by the disciples.

orig.note: Greek: a large basket; the word Acts 9:25 uses for Saul's escape.

carryVoice: Your line: barnabas took him, and told Saul's story when nobody else would. That's the day.
